notable_claims: Western Washington University removed the alt.sex newsgroup via administrative request.
The University of Washington resisted pressure to censor computer material and considered basing its selection policy on library standards.
classification.summary: The Electronic Frontier Foundation summarizes a controversy involving the presence of sexually explicit material on university computers in Washington state. While Central Washington University demoted an employee for private gain, the University of Washington resisted censorship pressure following media coverage. In response to the publicity, Western Washington University removed the alt.sex newsgroup by administrative request.
classification.title: U of Washington Summary

notable_claims: Western Washington University banned alt.sex newsgroups by classifying them as 'junk mail'.
The University of Washington stated it was not wise, legal, or proper to ban pornographic material on its equipment.
A director at Central Washington University was demoted due to the presence of pornographic files on Computer Center equipment.
classification.summary: Jeff Wandling reports the removal of alt.sex and alt.binary.pictures.erotica newsgroups from Western Washington University's USENET database. The action followed media reports regarding pornographic files at the University of Washington and a demotion at Central Washington University. While the University of Washington declined to ban such material, Western Washington University's Vice Provost classified it as 'junk mail' to justify the ban.
classification.title: alt.sex

notable_claims: The banning of alt.sex is a step toward restricting broader intellectual discourse on campuses.
Federal government funding for network environments could be used as leverage to censor controversial topics like abortion.
classification.summary: Daniel Mittleman expresses concern over the banning of the newsgroup alt.sex in Washington, arguing it sets a dangerous precedent for censorship. He suggests that such actions could lead to federal funding threats against universities that host controversial discourse on Usenet. The author argues this trend threatens the freedom of intellectual discourse on college campuses.
classification.title: Re: alt.sex

notable_claims: The removal of newsgroups by administrative request violates the ALA Library Bill of Rights.
Computer sites should follow established library procedures for the reconsideration and removal of controversial materials to protect intellectual freedom.
classification.summary: Carl Kadie argues that the removal of the 'alt.sex' newsgroup from Western Washington University via administrative request constitutes a violation of academic freedom. He draws a parallel between computer site newsgroup selection and traditional library magazine subscriptions, citing American Library Association (ALA) standards to argue against proscribing materials based on doctrinal disapproval.
classification.title: Re: USENET censorship strikes University of Washington!

identity.subject: Re: USENET censorship strikes University of Washington!

notable_claims: The Public Forum Doctrine is based on function rather than medium.
Campus BBS and Usenet facilities can be classified as limited public forums, restricting the state's ability to impose content-based prohibitions.
classification.summary: Carl Kadie argues that the Supreme Court's Public Forum Doctrine applies to campus digital communications like Usenet and BBS facilities. He provides legal precedents regarding school-sponsored publications to argue that state institutions cannot engage in content-based or viewpoint-based discrimination once a forum for expression has been established.
classification.title: Re: USENET censorship strikes University of Washington!

identity.subject: Re: USENET censorship strikes University of Washington!

notable_claims: Courts are generally reluctant to endorse prior restraints on student publications but more likely to support disciplinary action after distribution.
Discussion of controversial issues such as war, drugs, and abortion cannot be barred from student publications.
classification.summary: A discussion regarding the legality of university censorship of student publications and netnews. The post cites legal literature to distinguish between prior restraint and disciplinary action following distribution, specifically addressing libel, obscenity, and disruption of educational processes.
classification.title: Re: Netnews censorship at U. of Kentucky

identity.subject: Re: Netnews censorship at U. of Kentucky

notable_claims: The criteria for removing newsgroups should be identical to those for removing books from libraries.
Access to information subject only to cost limitations is an essential part of academic freedom.
Censorship is not an appropriate tool for dealing with offensive behavior.
classification.summary: John McCarthy describes a 1989 conflict at Stanford University regarding the suppression of the newsgroup rec.humor.funny. The Computer Science Department and the Committee on Libraries both argued that electronic newsgroups should be treated as library resources, asserting that censoring them is contrary to academic freedom.
classification.title: Censorship on the USENET

notable_claims: Computation centers may use library policies as a basis for newsgroup selection policies to prevent complaints.
classification.summary: John Hascall discusses the intersection of library collection policies and Usenet newsgroup management. He argues that computation centers should adopt established library policies to justify their content moderation decisions to complainants.

notable_claims: Users in the USSR used networks to coordinate resistance to the August 1991 coup.
Usenet allows simultaneous, diverse discussions (e.g., politics vs. physics) to occur without drowning each other out.
classification.summary: Douglas W. Jones discusses the utility of Usenet as a tool for political resistance and intellectual exchange. He highlights how network users in the USSR coordinated against the August 1991 coup and argues that electronic forums allow diverse, simultaneous discussions to coexist without interfering with one another.
classification.title: Re: What is good about Netnews/Usenet

identity.subject: Re: What is good about Netnews/Usenet

notable_claims: Selective censorship of newsgroups may make a university legally liable as a guarantor of the remaining information.
Hiding Usenet content from media attention to prevent restrictions is compared to trivializing the Constitution.
classification.summary: A discussion regarding the University of Washington's handling of pornography on its computers and the broader implications of Usenet censorship. Jamie Saker argues against hiding Usenet from the media to avoid a slippery slope toward book-burning and intellectual purging. Saker suggests that selective censorship may increase university liability by making them guarantors of content, recommending disclaimers instead.
classification.title: Re: USENET censorship strikes University of Washington!

identity.subject: Re: USENET censorship strikes University of Washington!

notable_claims: A rogue user with a stolen account transposted alt.sex messages to k12.chat.* newsgroups.
The Texas Education Network (TENET) shut down Usenet access shortly after implementation due to this incident.
Appropriate use is cited by NSF network directors as one of the most significant issues facing the community.
classification.summary: Janet Murray provides background on a 'porno incident' involving K12Net and the Texas Education Network (TENET). She clarifies that adult content was cross-posted to educational newsgroups by a rogue user with a stolen University of Washington account, rather than being generated by students. The exchange highlights early tensions regarding 'appropriate use' policies and the risk of overreacting to isolated incidents by shutting down network access.
classification.title: Re: So what is the answer?
